name: Local churches (Little Flock)

citations.locator: China, Christianity in, New Catholic Encyclopedia (J.-P. Wiest)
citations.excerpt: The Chinese Independent Church began in 1906, the True Jesus Church in 1917, the Jesus Family in 1921, and the Little Flock in 1922.

citations.locator: Other Bible Students: The (Local) Church, Encyclopedia of American Religions
citations.excerpt: The group that is variously known as the Little Flock or the Local Church was founded in the 1920s in China by Ni Shutsu, popularly known by the English translation of his name, Watchman Nee (1903-1972).

citations.locator: Other Bible Students: The (Local) Church, Encyclopedia of American Religions

facts.value: One local church in each city as the expression of the unity of the church. No clergy-laity distinction. The movement takes no denominational name

citations.locator: Other Bible Students: The (Local) Church, Encyclopedia of American Religions
citations.excerpt: founded congregations based upon his idea that there should be only one local church (i.e., congregation) in each city as the basic expression of the unity of Christianity (in the face of divisive denominationalism).

citations.locator: Other Bible Students: The (Local) Church, Encyclopedia of American Religions
citations.excerpt: In rejecting the clergy-laity distinction, a pattern for the practical expression of the church's life has been established.

citations.locator: Other Bible Students: The (Local) Church, Encyclopedia of American Religions
citations.excerpt: The Local Church sees itself as simply the Church. The term "local church" is a convenient designation but not a name.

facts.value: Nee adopted the nondenominational church approach of John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren. Nee was arrested in 1952 and held for the rest of his life. Nee sent Witness Lee to Taiwan, where the church spread around the Pacific Basin. Migrating members brought it to the West Coast of the United States

research_notes: Addition pass 2026-10-28 (Eric msg 1565087303565840456). Lane free: ARDA classes The Local Churches under the Evangelical Protestant tradition, and Melton (Encyclopedia of American Religions) records belief in the Trinity, the deity of Christ and other fundamental Christian doctrines. No approved source places it outside the historic creeds. Concise Oxford calls it 'Christian-based', which is not such a classification. Lane parent g113 Plymouth Brethren because Melton states the movement developed out of the Plymouth Brethren (excerpt in description). No split_from fact: sources describe influence, not a formal separation. ARDA profile https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=1308 gives no description or founding date. Names 'Christian Assembly' not found in an approved source, omitted.
